item.title: NFL Monday Night Football preview: Rams, without Myles Garrett and perhaps Puka Nacua too, already in big spot vs. Giants
item.description: The Rams and Giants had much different results in Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for the Los Angeles Rams to go from the most popular preseason Super Bowl pick to feeling a little desperate.

The first days of the season have been bad for the Rams. They had an ugly 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia. After the game, defensive end Myles Garrett had knee surgery, went on injured reserve and doesn't have a timetable for return. Then receiver Puka Nacua popped up on the injury report with a hip injury and a report from ESPN's Adam Schefter on Sunday said his status is trending in the "wrong direction" for Monday night's game against the New York Giants.

So in less than two weeks the Rams lost their opener with practically every player performing below their standard, then lost arguably the best defensive player in the NFL for a stretch and might have to be without one of the league's best offensive players against the Giants.

The Giants don't look like a pushover this season either. New York was excellent in its opener against the Dallas Cowboys, which was a 28-20 win. The Giants offense had an efficient night, controlling the ball for 36:40, and the defense did a good job controlling Dallas' offense. There were evident changes in the first game of the John Harbaugh era.

The Rams have already seen the Seahawks and 49ers start the season 2-0 in the NFC West. Falling to 0-2 in one of the NFL's toughest divisions would be an early hole the Rams never expected to find themselves in. But without two of the NFL's best players, against a Giants team that looked much improved in its opener, it's a possibility for the Rams at the start of what was supposed to be a championship season.

Who needs it more?

Even with Myles Garrett out and Puka Nacua possibly out as well, the Rams are favored to win by a touchdown. The Giants could lose on the road to a team that is still the Super Bowl betting favorite and be fine with a promising 1-1 start. The Rams would not be fine with an 0-2 start while battling some key injuries, with the Seahawks and 49ers looking great in their division. It's hard to call any game in Week 2 a must win, especially for a team as good as the Rams, but another loss would not be great. Their upcoming schedule is at Denver, at Philadelphia, vs. Bills. An 0-2 start could become 1-4 or worse. There's a lot more pressure on Los Angeles this Monday night.

Key player: Giants TE Isaiah Likely

It was significant that the Giants, with John Harbaugh in charge, signed the tight end who he had in Baltimore but never broke out because he was behind Mark Andrews. Likely showed his promise when he played, then he signed a three-year, $40 million deal with Harbaugh's new team. In the season opener, Likely played a huge role with eight catches for 78 yards and two touchdowns. It seemed like every time Jaxson Dart needed a key play, he was looking Likely's way. Four of Likely's catches came on third downs, converting all four into first downs, and two came in the red zone. Malik Nabers is still a bit limited as he returns from a torn ACL, though he had six catches for 69 yards in the opener. The pressure is not entirely on Nabers to carry the passing game, because Likely is already a big factor.

Betting market watch, by Ben Fawkes

This game will be a study in perception, as the Giants are coming off an impressive win last Sunday night over the Cowboys, while the Rams couldn't have looked much worse in Australia in a blowout loss to the 49ers. Los Angeles has also lost Myles Garrett for several weeks and star WR Puka Nacua is questionable to play in this game, so we've seen the line dip from Rams -7.5 in the offseason to -6.5. The betting public is taking the points with New York, but I'd preach caution. Heading into this weekend, the Rams were still the highest power-rated team in the NFL, according to oddsmakers I spoke with, and one bad game doesn't make a season. Watch out for a thin Giants cornerback rotation as well, with Paulson Adebo out and Deonte Banks questionable. Look for Los Angeles to get back on track tonight and cover this spread.

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Fantasy football storylines, by Scott Pianowski

Many fantasy matchups will be settled as the Rams and Giants wrap up Week 2. Here are three fantasy angles to keep in mind as you watch the game.

1. What is the second pitch in the Rams passing game? Puka Nacua will either play this game at less than 100% or miss it entirely. He was the only Los Angeles player to go over 26 yards receiving in the opener. It's essential for Davante Adams, Terrance Ferguson and others to step up here, with or without Nacua.

2. Can Jaxson Dart play another clean game? Dart took just two sacks and had zero turnovers as the Giants controlled the clock and took care of Dallas in Week 1. Dart's challenge is far greater against this Los Angeles defense, even with the Rams missing Myles Garrett. If Dart is on point, Isaiah Likely (8-78-2 in the opener) is capable of furthering a breakout season.

3. What is the backfield split for the Rams? Kyren Willams had 14 touches in the opener, while Blake Corum handled 10. Corum's success rate was higher, but Williams had more receiving work and also punched in a short touchdown. A healthy Williams will be a fantasy staple all year, but the emerging Corum could push for RB3 territory right away — and would be an automatic starter later in the year if Williams were to get hurt.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers, Mike McCarthy see the issues with the Pittsburgh offense
item.description: When he's complaining about Anthony Fauci, ESPN, and/or Shailene Woodley, Aaron Rodgers is not subtle.
item.content:encoded:
When he's complaining about Anthony Fauci, ESPN, and/or Shailene Woodley, Aaron Rodgers is not subtle. When he has concerns about his football team, his criticisms are harder to pinpoint.

But they're still there.

After Sunday's loss to the Patriots, Rodgers dropped a hint or two regarding coach Mike McCarthy's offense. And Rodgers did it in a way that will give him plausible deniability if someone else spots it and points it out.

"In a game like today where there wasn't a lot of flow to it, we need to be better," Rodgers told reporters after the 20-6 loss. "And that starts with me at like making sure Mike knows what's working, what's not working, our coaches know, and — so we can call stuff that we feel like has a better chance."

In other words, some of the "stuff" McCarthy was calling didn't have a very good chance.

When asked later about things that are "working" and "not working," Rodgers said, "The plays were fine." But he then suggested that perhaps the offense was overloaded with plays.

"If there's too much stuff in the plan, we've got to cut it back," Rodgers said. "I'm always liking to push the envelope, and if I see guys doing it the right way in practice, then I feel good about it, but we've got to transfer the practice to the game obviously and the details gotta come with it."

The hidden criticisms aren't off-base; McCarthy himself made similar comments about the size of the game plan.

"We've got to look at the volume," he told reporters after the game. "That's Marty Schottenheimer, that was his thing. It was a great lesson for a young coach to learn, and here I am some old bastard that didn't do it this week. If it's not clean, you cut the volume down, and we're not clean on offense.

"So the volume is getting cut down. That's the first starting point, and that's my fault. I felt it earlier in the week. We've got a quarterback that could play at any volume of game plan, but at the end of the day, it's a team game. We've got to give Aaron better platforms to throw off of and have the opportunities because I don't want to dink and dunk and play all day and play keep-away football."

McCarthy's remarks on the volume of the game plan came after he attributed the offensive struggles to things he had observed during the week.

"Felt it in practice frankly, coming off of last week," McCarthy said. "As I stated, I felt we were real herky-jerky trying to get in the run and pass. . . . The run game was a little bit herky-jerky. . . . But the reality of it is the detail is not there, and that's on coaching. It starts with me. I'm calling the offense. I have to get the detail better. . . . I felt it on Wednesday and Thursday. I'm a veteran coach. I know better. I didn't do a good job."

McCarthy was asked to clarify his comment about "feeling it" during the week.

"Just volume," McCarthy said. "We've done this a long time. You know when the volume is up, and you know when you're pushing the envelope too. It's also the first year of the staff and players working together. So you want to push your players, but end of the day, you've got to do it to win a game."

Rodgers has faith McCarthy will make the fixes that need to be made.

"I've seen Mike for 14 years. So, Mike is going to take accountability, sometimes when it's not his fault, doesn't need to do that," Rodgers said. "But Mike loves the guys, and he wants us to have some urgency and to bounce back with this, and I know we will."

They need to. The offense has engineered one touchdown drive in two full games, and it covered only 31 yards. The Steelers easily could have lost to the Falcons in Week 1, and the Falcons looked horrible in Week 2.

In six days, the 2-0 Bengals come to Pittsburgh. And while the Steelers tend to find a way to win certain key games, it becomes a much taller task if the offense isn't delivering.

At some point, Rodgers himself has to deliver. He's completing fewer than 60 percent of his passes (his career average is 65.1), he's averaging only 5.2 yards per attempt (down from 6.7 in 2025), and his passer rating is a very sluggish 72.1. Rodgers has never had a full-season rating below 90.5, and that happened during his 5-12 final year with the Jets.

item.title: Fantasy Football Stock Report: Chargers' offense looks lost while Panthers' unit continues to thrive going into Week 3
item.description: Matt Okada takes you through the biggest risers and fallers after Week 2 for fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
As I write this on Sunday night, 15 of 16 Week 2 games are in the books (with Monday night remaining) and the season's second week looked ... completely different from its first. There were promising improvements, concerning trends and performances that changed our early outlook on players and teams. As always, some of these shifting perspectives will have permanent ramifications in fantasy football.

With that in mind, I've compiled another full fantasy stock report. These are the most notable risers and fallers heading into Week 3. 

Stock Up

Dalton Kincaid, TE, Bills

Frankly, Dalton Kincaid isn't just the top "Stock Up" player of this week. He's arguably the top "Stock Up" player in all of fantasy, relative to his summer draft price. He's made a legitimate two-week case as the top tight end behind Trey McBride and Brock Bowers (when he's eventually healthy). After a monster 130-yard performance in Week 1, Kincaid caught seven of eight targets for 95 yards and a touchdown in Week 2 on TNF.

Most importantly, he tied Keon Coleman for the most routes on the team (26), the nail in the coffin of years of previously head-scratching usage in Buffalo. That full-time usage now unlocks what has always been elite efficiency for the Bills tight end — since he was drafted in 2023, Kincaid's 2.0 yards per route run is second to George Kittle among all tight ends with 300+ routes. Kincaid is one of the best weapons for the league's best quarterback in what is almost certainly the league's best offense. He's an elite fantasy asset, period, full stop.

DeVonta Smith, WR, Eagles

The second game of the post-A.J. Brown era revealed a version of DeVonta Smith we certainly didn't see in Week 1 and have rarely seen before. The Eagles' No. 1 receiver saw 13 targets — a 38% share — and caught 10 of them for 117 yards and a touchdown. That tied Smith's previous career high in targets (from the 2022 season) and matched his second-best reception total, positioning him to be a top-five scoring wideout on the week entering Monday Night Football. But perhaps most importantly, he looked the part throughout the game, making a number of true WR1 catches, most notably this snag with the game on the line on third down, to set up the walk-off score. Smith has a juicy matchup with the Bears in Week 3, where he could cement his place as a high-end WR2 with another performance like Sunday's.

TreVeyon Henderson, RB, Patriots

It was a near-perfect storm for TreVeyon Henderson as he returned from a Week 1 injury absence. Running mate Rhamondre Stevenson coughed up another troubling fumble, Henderson ripped off an explosive 39-yard touchdown run and the volume split finished 16 touches to seven in the younger back's favor. Stevenson has now fumbled 18 times since he was drafted in 2021, most by any non-QB in the entire NFL.

Considering how much more explosive and effective Henderson has looked as a runner, this trend could threaten to relegate Stevenson to pass-protection snaps and a complementary receiving role. That would give Henderson an open lane to RB1 usage in what should be a great offense (though Drake Maye and Co. have seemed a little wobbly to start the season). Henderson isn't a locked-and-loaded RB2 yet ... but another game or two like this one and he'll be there quick.

Jaylen Waddle & Jonah Coleman, WR/RB, Broncos

While these two "Stock Ups" are largely unrelated — outside of being on the same team — I'm combining them here for efficiency! Let's start with Waddle. Outside of an absurdly disappointing two-yard season opener that had fantasy drafters in shambles, Waddle rebounded to the tune of eight catches for 138 yards on 10 targets against the Jaguars. He was targeted on 42% of the routes he ran in this game and snagged a 49-yard catch that landed him on the one-yard line ... inches away from an extra 6 fantasy points. Waddle's back in WR2 range after what will likely be remembered as an aberrant Week 1.

As for rookie running back Jonah Coleman, he took over when J.K. Dobbins exited with a hamstring injury — as RJ Harvey was inactive with his own hamstring injury — and took his 13 opportunities for 58 yards and a goal-line rushing touchdown. You might remember Coleman from the All-Sleeper Team two weeks ago, where I highlighted the potential he has to simply take the job in Denver. The door is creaking open, and it wouldn't be surprising to see the rookie atop the depth chart in the very near future.

Panthers' offense

To put it simply, the entire Panthers offense looks great coming off a 34-3 trouncing of the rival Falcons. Bryce Young followed a 361-yard, four-TD performance against the Bears in the opener with a 287-yard, three-TD encore on Sunday. He's second in the NFL in passing yards (to Tyler Shough), has a 113.3 passer rating and has thrown six touchdowns to just one interception. And it's thanks in large part to his finally dangerous receiving corps, as Tetairoa McMillan hit 101 yards in Week 2, while Jalen Coker raised his season totals to 16 catches for 204 yards.

Plus, Chuba Hubbard caught a receiving touchdown for a second straight week (and has 151 yards on 27 touches) and tight end Darren Waller snagged two touchdown grabs of his own against Atlanta. Carolina's offense will face a real test next Sunday in Cleveland — after drawing the Bears and Falcons the first two weeks — but Young and Co. look extremely improved on tape and in the stat sheet. After two-and-a-half to three years of mostly mediocrity, it appears they've finally arrived.

Stock Down

Chargers' passing game

The Chargers lost 26-14 to the Cardinals in Week 1, a team that had three wins last season. But that couldn't happen again in Week 2, right? Welp. They lost 26-14 to the Raiders, another three-win team from a season ago. No, I'm not joking. They made the kind of history you never want to make, and Justin Herbert looks completely lost in Mike McDaniel's offense.

The Chargers are the second team in NFL history to lose back-to-back games by double digits with both coming at home against teams that had a sub-.200 win pct the previous season.

The other was the 1926 Racine Tornadoes (Oct. 10-17), who played just one more game before folding.

— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) September 21, 2026

Through two weeks, Herbert has thrown two touchdown passes and three interceptions, not to mention the three fumbles he committed on Sunday alone (none of which, miraculously, were recovered by Las Vegas). The Chargers only reached the red zone twice in Week 2, with nine of their 13 drives ending in their own territory (including a game-ending safety). Ladd McConkey was surprisingly active for the game, but had just three targets and 5.0 fantasy points, while Quentin Johnston totaled one catch for seven yards on his five targets. Los Angeles is going to have some serious soul-searching to do before a terrifying matchup with the Bills in Week 3 ... but until the Chargers find whatever they're looking for, Herbert and his receivers could be very tough to trust.

Bears' pass-catchers

A week after everything went right for the Bears in Week 1 ... absolutely nothing did in Week 2. They scored just three points against the Vikings and Caleb Williams suffered a hamstring injury that seemed severe when it went down. We're still waiting on the timeline and long-term impact of that injury, and Tyson Bagent is a serviceable backup, but it has not looked great for Rome Odunze, Luther Burden III or Colston Loveland either way.

Odunze has just five catches on seven targets this season, despite running essentially all the routes. Burden's usage has been disappointing and he's shown no sign of the breakout many had expected entering the season. And Loveland ... oof. The TE3 in draft ADP has one catch for three yards on five targets through two weeks. Tight ends with more fantasy points so far include Will Kacmarek and Jake Briningstool (Yes, those are real people). Stay tuned for the Williams news — and for future games in better weather against softer defenses — but the fact that Kalif Raymond is the top fantasy pass-catcher on this team is not great news for managers.

Drake Maye, QB, Patriots

The optimistic perspective on Drake Maye after two weeks is that the early struggles can be blamed on the loss of A.J. Brown — after planning the offense around his acquisition — and that Maye will rebound on his return. But Brown or no Brown, it's pretty hard to explain Maye's one TD pass and four interceptions through two games. In all of 2025, Maye threw for fewer than 210 passing yards just three times. He's already done so twice in two games in 2026.

This week against Pittsburgh, he completed just 14 passes, was sacked three times and posted a 75.6 passer rating. He's sitting at just 21.8 fantasy points after Week 2, barely ahead of Aaron Rodgers and behind Jacoby Brissett, Cam Ward and Carson Wentz, among others. Maye could get into a barn-burner against the Jaguars next week, so you're probably still starting him (and hoping) for at least another couple games. But, right now, we are simply not seeing the breakout quarterback who led the Patriots to 14 wins last season.

Terry McLaurin, WR, Commanders

With the elbow injury to Jayden Daniels — who does not have a timeline yet as I write this on Sunday night — I was initially tempted to "Stock Down" the entire Washington offense, or at least their entire receiving corps. However, I think the move to Marcus Mariota, for however long it lasts, is more specifically concerning for Terry McLaurin. For one thing, McLaurin has already not looked like the team's clear WR1 through two games: he has fewer targets (13) than Stefon Diggs (15), while Diggs (9), Rachaad White (8), Antonio Williams (7) and Dyami Brown (4) all have as many or more catches than McLaurin (4). McLaurin has an abysmal 30.8% catch rate and has honestly become something of an Alec Pierce, with high route participation and an incredibly high aDOT (14.4 air yards), but very little (if any) reliability. Mariota will take occasional downfield shots but is not going to be the solve for McLaurin's efficiency problems. And while Diggs can find relative consistency in a PPR role in the meantime — and caught a 20-yard touchdown from Mariota on Sunday — I worry McLaurin will be incredibly hit-or-miss for the foreseeable future.

David Montgomery, RB, Texans

A week after going berserk with three touchdowns in his Texans debut, David Montgomery totaled 10 rushing yards on six carries and finished Week 2 with 3.4 fantasy points. And while the Bengals' defense looks much improved, there's very little excuse or silver lining in 1.7 yards per carry amid a blowout loss. Worst of all, Woody Marks actually outcarried Montgomery eight to six ... though he was, incredibly, even less efficient, with just eight yards on those eight carries.

Unfortunately, the reality with Montgomery is that he'll probably mix-and-match these types of outings all year. When he finds the end zone, he'll be a strong RB2. When he doesn't, and particularly when the Texans fall behind, he'll likely have a series of fantasy duds. Montgomery thrived with his particular skill set when playing for the Lions' high-scoring, ever-in-the-red-zone offense. The Texans are not that. And it's going to reflect poorly in the running back's box score throughout the year.

item.title: Arizona Cardinals Daily Links: Has patience run out for Marvin Harrison Jr.?
item.description: Marvin Harrison has just four targets through the team’s first two games of the 2026 season.
item.content:encoded:
It is year three for Marvin Harrison Jr. and we’re two games into the season. His current stat line is just one reception for 33 yards. That is far, far from what many would have expected now that he’s healthy to begin a season while boasting two years of NFL experience, regardless of how up-and-down they have been.

But the NFL is a “what have you one for me lately?” business and when players go too long without being able to offer a strong response to that question, things tend to spiral in the wrong direction.

Can Marv find a way to turn it around despite this lackluster start? Is this just a bad blip on the radar and he just needs more time? Is there such a thing as giving him more time in year three? Sure feels like history is not going to be kind to his current career path, but we’ve all seen crazier things happen in the NFL.

item.title: Packers’ win over Jets was the 3rd double-digit comeback win in the Jordan Love era
item.description: The Packers have come from ten points down to win 10 times total under Matt LaFleur.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers managed to flip the script on Sunday afternoon. After giving up big lead after big lead down the stretch on the 2025 season and in Week 1 against the Minnesota Vikings, the Packers came back from a ten-point deficit in the fourth quarter to defeat the New York Jets 20-17 in Week 2.

A post by our friends at the Cro Pack Cro podcast after last week’s game now seems like an odd and amusing omen:

Still, this post got me to thinking last week, so I did some research ahead of the Week 2 game. Since Jordan Love took over as the Packers’ full-time starting quarterback to start the 2023 season, the Packers had exactly two comeback wins when down by 10 or more points at any time in the game before Sunday’s win at MetLife Stadium, which became the third.

Prior to Love’s tenure, however, the Packers successfully mounting big comebacks was a bit more common. In the four seasons with LaFleur as head coach and Aaron Rodgers at quarterback the team posted seven wins after facing a double-digit deficit.

Let’s look at the first two Love comebacks first, then we’ll take a quick look at the earlier ones from the LaFleur-Rodgers era.

2023 Week 3: vs. New Orleans Saints

Love’s third start of the 2023 season and his fourth start overall got out to an abysmal start. Facing an Alvin Kamara-less Saints squad, the Packers dug themselves a 17-0 hole by halftime thanks to touchdowns by former Packer Jimmy Graham and a punt return score from Rasheed Shaheed.

Rashan Gary had his first and only three-sack game in this contest, however, and one of those knocked starting QB Derek Carr out of the game early in the third quarter. The score remained 17-0 heading into the fourth quarter, however, when the Packers eked out a field goal to finally get on the board.

Green Bay’s leading receiver in the game was the Defensive Pass Interference flag. Love drew back-to-back DPI calls on the first two plays of the next drive, first a 45-yarder on Alontae Taylor then a 22-yard call on Isaac Yiadom. Love eventually ran the ball into the end zone on 4th-and-goal from the 1 to pull the Packers to within 8 points at 17-9, and LaFleur made the decision to go for two. Love converted with a pass to Samori Touré, bringing Green Bay back to within six points and giving them a chance to win with a touchdown.

The defense forced a 3-and-out, and Love led the offense on another touchdown drive, picking up 24 yards on a scramble and a 30-yard gain on a pass to Jayden Reed. Love eventually found Romeo Doubs for an 8-yard touchdown on 3rd down and Anders Carlson hit the PAT to put the Packers ahead.

The drama wasn’t over, however. The Packers’ win was not secured until a few minutes later, when Blake Grupe’s 46-yard go-ahead field goal attempt went wide right.

2025 Week 7: @ Arizona Cardinals

The most recent 10-point comeback came last year in one of the crazier games of the 2025 season. You might not even remember that the Packers were down by double digits, however, because they only trailed by that amount of time for SEVEN SECONDS.

The Cardinals took a 13-3 lead with 0:07 left in the second quarter, as Trey McBride scored a touchdown to give them that edge. Arizona booted the kickoff into the end zone, however, and one 22-yard completion from Love to Romeo Doubs over the middle and a timeout brought Lucas Havrisik on for a franchise-record 61-yard field goal to pull the Packers to within 13-6 at halftime. Green Bay then doubled up and tied the game on the first drive of the third quarter and traded scores throughout the second half, eventually winning 27-23 after Matt LaFleur kept his offense on the field late rather than kicking to tie the game.

Remember that 4th down conversion to Tucker Kraft? We sure did, as it ranked #9 on our Top Plays of 2025 Countdown. This whole game was well-represented on that countdown, with Havrisik’s franchise record kick landing at #8 and a game-clinching sack from Micah Parsons earning an honorable mention.

That’s three comebacks in just over three seasons of Love, but in the four years of the LaFleur-Rodgers, the Packers mounted seven such wins. Many of these were early deficits, however, not late rallies. In fact, only four of these games saw the Packers trail at any point in the fourth quarter.

2019 Week 6: vs. Lions

The first double-digit comeback for Matt LaFleur as head coach was in his first game against the Lions early in the 2019 season. Detroit led 13-0 early in the second quarter before the Packers stormed back, tying the game on the first drive of the second half. The Lions kicked three straight field goals after that to take back a 9-point lead early in the fourth quarter, but Allen Lazard’s heroics — scoring on a 35-yard touchdown and hauling in three big receptions on the final drive of the game — helped set up Mason Crosby for a short game-winning field goal for a 23-22 victory.

2019 Week 17: @ Lions

The Packers came back on Matt Patricia’s Lions in both 2019 matchups. With David Blough starting at quarterback, Detroit led 17-3 at the half, getting a field goal on a 20-second drive before the break. As in the previous matchup, Lazard scored a 4th-quarter touchdown, this time to tie the game at 20, and Crosby again gave the Packers the win as the clock expired. That sent the Packers into the playoffs at 13-3 and as the NFC’s second seed.

2020 Week 2: vs. Lions

It was 3-for-3 in comeback wins for LaFleur against Patricia. Once again, Detroit led 14-3, this time at the end of the first quarter, but Green Bay stormed back with 31 unanswered points, including two Rodgers touchdown passes, a 75-yard score from Aaron Jones, and a pick-six by Chandon Sullivan, cruising to a 42-21 win.

2021 Week 14: vs. Bears

It was a season and a half between big comebacks for the Packers, who trailed 10-0 to Chicago early in the second quarter on Sunday Night Football. The Packers bounced back with back-to-back scores, including a Rasul Douglas pick-six, but they gave the Bears two right back on a long pass from Fields to Damiere Byrd and then a 97-yard punt return by Jakeem Grant as the Bears retook a 10-point lead at 24-14. The Packers got a touchdown before the half from Davante Adams, then the Bears tacked on a field goal before the break, holding a 27-21 lead at halftime.

After that, though, it was all Packers, as they cleaned up their issues and outscored the Bears 24-3 in the second half, eventually closing out a 45-30 victory.

2022 Week 10: vs. Cowboys

The Packers, facing old head coach Mike McCarthy for the first time, were down 28-14 to start the fourth quarter. Aaron Rodgers found Christian Watson for two 4th-quarter scores to send the game to overtime, then they got a 4th down stop with the Cowboys in Packers territory and Mason Crosby kicked a short field goal to win the game 31-28.

2022 Week 12: @ Bears

An eventual 28-19 Packers win started out poorly, with Chicago going up 10-0 in the first quarter. Justin Fields provided the early Bears touchdown with a 55-yard run and the Bears led 19-10 heading into the fourth, but the Packers were driving at the time. AJ Dillon scored on the second play of the fourth quarter to cut the lead to two, then the Packers got a go-ahead field goal from Crosby before Watson put the game away with a 46-yard run on an end-around for the final score of a 9-point win.

2022 Week 16: vs. Dolphins

The Packers may have only won 8 games in 2022, but three of them were of the big comeback variety. On Christmas Day, the Dolphins took a 20-10 lead late in the second quarter with Green Bay’s defense struggling to contain Jaylen Waddle (an 84-yard score early, 143 total yards) and Tyreek Hill (104 receiving yards). However, Miami went into full collapse mode after that.

The Dolphins final five possessions went as follows: lost fumble, missed field goal, interception, interception, interception. That allowed the Packers to put up three field goals and a touchdown unanswered in a 26-20 victory.

item.title: Cowboys vs. Commanders: The good, bad, and ugly from Week 2
item.description: The Cowboys won which was great, but there are definitely things to clean up.
item.content:encoded:
Compared to their embarrassing loss to the New York Giants last week inthe season opener, the Dallas Cowboys look like an entirely different team in their 37-20 victory over the Washington Commanders in Week 2. With a chance they could drop 0-2 in the NFC East division if they lost, the Cowboys came out and played with purpose in front of their hometown crowd and did what they needed to do in order to secure the “W”.

Despite the much-needed victory, this was probably a closer game in the score reflects. This hard-fought victory that had a lot of positives and negatives mixed throughout the ballgame. Fortunately, things bounced the Cowboys way this time around, resulting in their first win on the season. Below is the good, bad, and ugly from this week’s matchup.

THE GOOD – QB Dak Prescott, WR CeeDee Lamb

Shout out to Jake Ferguson for his four catches for 43 yards and two touchdowns. He definitely deserves recognition here, but it’s Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb who helped propel this team to victory.

Prescott set a franchise record with 249 TD passes, eclipsing Tony Romo’s record. He threw for four of them during the game. Lamb caught a total of eight passes for 153 receiving yards and two touchdowns Sunday afternoon against the Commanders. There’s a reason why Dallas has leaned on him so heavily in the past, and this week was proof why he’s so important despite the multitude of weapon surrounding him.

This offense runs through No. 4 and No. 88, and are at their best when they are productive.

THE BAD – Christian Parker’s defense

Compared to last week in the season opener, the Cowboys defense looked much improved in Week 2 against the Commanders. They did enough to help secure the victory and in the end that’s all that matters. However, there is still clearly a lot of work to do for Christian Parker.

Dallas’ run defense still looks suspect and the tackling throughout was pretty abysmal. In fact, Donovan Eziruaku left at least three QB sacks on the field by not finishing. Overall though this was a much better showing and one that hopefully continues to improve week to week.

THE UGLY – Injuries

On the Commanders side of things, QB Jayden Daniels suffered an ugly injury as he dislocated his elbow. He had to miss half the game, and will probably miss more times as he tries to recover. The out-of-place elbow certainly looked gruesome.

For Dallas, first it was P.J. Locke who exited the game with a foot injury, and then Cobie Durant with a hamstring injury. With Malik Hooker already out several weeks with a forearm injury, Locke’s further depletes the safety position. The same can be said at CB if Durant ends up having to miss time.

item.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints win against the Ravens
item.description: Saints come from behind in Baltimore to grab a win against one of the NFL’s best teams
item.content:encoded:
The Good: Tyler Shough and Chris Olave

Shough and Olave once again had a great day, as Shough threw for 252 yards and Olave went for 86 yards while the pair connected for the game tying touchdown. Juwan Johnson and Devaughn Vele also had very good days, as they each converted a few tough third downs and had 60+ receiving yards in their own right. Shough is the NFL’s passing yards leader through two games and Olave trails only Jaxon Smith-Njigba in receiving yards. This combination is only going to continue to get better as the season goes along, as after two tough road games to start the year the Saints now have three very winnable games in the Superdome over the next three weeks before they head to New York and then Paris.

The Bad: Rushing offense

The Saints trailed much of the game, so they did not need to rely on the ground game that much, but even still they did not produce much in that area this week. As a team they ran 27 times for 65 yards which is an average of 2.4 yards per carry. This is going to be a problem if they manage to get a lead early in some of their next few games against weaker opponents and need to milk the clock a bit, as so far through two weeks the Saints and new addition Travis Etienne Jr. are averaging just 3 yards per carry on the ground. The Ravens and Lions both have above average run defenses, but still we need to see a bit more considering how good we know Etienne and Alvin Kamara can be.

The Ugly: Another slow start

The Saints started slow again on Sunday, thankfully not as slow as they did last week in Detroit but they still eventually needed a +15 point fourth quarter to secure the win. The defense kept it close throughout as they had a very good day and deserve a lot of recognition for the win. The offense managed just three field goals through the first three quarters before turning it on in the fourth. They did not have any turnovers like last week but only had one drive of more than 50 yards before the fourth quarter. While exciting, this is a dangerous game to be playing week in and week out, and lets hope that the Saints returning home against lesser competition will have them take and hold a lead throughout a game rather than having to rely on fourth quarter comebacks most of the time.

item.title: To kick, or not to kick? NFL's new OT rules leave coaches with tough choice
item.description: The NFL's new OT rules have created a decision for coaches about whether to take the ball or play defense first in overtime. Which is the better choice?
item.content:encoded:
To kick, or not to kick? That is the question many NFL coaches are facing as a part of the league's relatively new regular-season overtime rules.

Under previous iterations of the NFL's overtime rules, the easy choice was to receive the ball after winning the opening coin toss. That would give teams a chance to end the game in sudden death, whether it was with a field goal in the rule-set that existed prior to 2012 or with a touchdown with the procedures that came after it.

But under the new rule set, teams are each guaranteed a possession in the extra period. That has led to an extra element of strategy for coaches as they try to earn overtime victories.

There is not yet an orthodoxy about how to approach overtime under the new rules. They are still in their infancy, which has led coaches to adopt varying strategies as they continue to test the waters and gather more data.

NFL fans got a taste of that firsthand in Week 2 of the 2026 season. There were two overtime games, and the coin-toss-winning teams – the New York Jets and Indianapolis Colts – from each contest chose different methods approaches to the extra, 10-minute period.

Here's more to know about the decisions of Aaron Glenn and Shane Steichen in those key moments.

To take the ball

Glenn and the Jets were the first team tasked with an overtime decision in Week 2. New York won the coin toss in its game against the Green Bay Packers and opted to take the ball first.

Glenn's decision to play offense first was predicated on a desire to control the clock during overtime, as he explained during a postgame news conference.

"Usually, if you can get yourself in a situation like that and you can really control the clock, you can control exactly how they're going to play offense once you go and score," Glenn told reporters. "So, we control the clock, we go run it down; say we run it seven minutes, which we’ve done before, we've run a number of time off the clock, it only gives them so much time to try to rebuttal."

Glenn lamented his team's execution with that strategy – he said they "didn’t do a good job in that situation" – but still expressed his belief in the Jets' strategy.

"Once you get the ball and you go down and score, you put the pressure on the other team that has to go ahead and score," Glenn said. "But that didn’t happen for us the way I planned."

Glenn further acknowledged that his staff works in tandem with the Jets' analytics staffers "quite a bit" to map out the best strategy for overtime.

The 54-year-old also expressed confidence in the Jets' strategy, which he noted was one of many unique philosophies about overtime from around the league.

"I take it back to the Tennessee game. We had that 19-play drive. We ran all that time off the clock," Glenn said, referencing the Jets' Week 1 win over the Titans. "To get a chance to go down and score and put pressure on the other team, I thought defensively, we were doing a pretty good job. I mean, that's a powerful, powerful offense. So, I just put those two things together and come up with my decision."

Glenn's strategy was understandable. If the team had achieved his desired result of control the clock and giving the Packers little time in which to mount a rebuttal, his decision would have been viewed favorably.

Instead, the Jets went three-and-out on their opening possession of overtime and did not get the ball back after punting it to the Packers. Rookie Trey Smack kicked a game-winning, 26-yard field goal to give the Packers a 20-17 win that thrusted Glenn's decision into the spotlight.

To not take the ball

While Glenn decided to take the ball to start overtime, Steichen and the Colts made the opposite decision in their "Sunday Night Football" win over the Kansas City Chiefs.

Steichen explained during his postgame news conference his decision about whether to take the ball in overtime "goes back and forth," depending on the situation. Against Kansas City, his choice to play defense was to avoid giving Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs extra downs with which to work.

"If we go first with it, Mahomes gets four downs going the other way, so we wanted to play defense there and know we had four downs to know what we gonna get," Steichen said. "It can go either way in those situations, but we decided to kick off there, and obviously, we had a chance there at the end. Didn’t finish it."

That Steichen would want to limit Mahomes' playmaking opportunities was sensible. Giving the three-time Super Bowl champion an extra down with which to work would have afforded him more opportunities to make the explosive plays fans have been accustomed to seeing him make across his time in Kansas City.

Of course, the caveat to this is that while Steichen's decision provided a buffer to the Chiefs having all four downs available, Kansas City did earn an extra possession after Indianapolis was only able to tie its intraconference rival on its lone possession of overtime. That allowed the Chiefs to mount a game-winning drive as time expired in overtime, with Harrison Butker hitting a walk-off 40-yard field goal to seal a 33-30 win.

One could make the case that had the Colts taken the ball first, the Chiefs would have had just one opportunity to beat them. But at the same time, a case can be made that had Indianapolis just executed better in the red-zone during overtime, the Colts would have emerged as the winners.

Instead, Mahomes was able to improve his regular-season overtime record to an impressive 8-0.

So, what's the right call?

It's still early to say which strategy will prove to be the best option long-term. There have thus far been just 16 regular-season games decided in overtime under the new rules entering "Monday Night Football" in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season. Meanwhile, three postseason games have gone to overtime since the new rules debuted during the 2022 NFL playoffs.

Below is a look at the record of the team's receiving the ball first:

  • Regular season: 9-7-1
  • Postseason: 2-1

And here's how teams playing defense first have fared:

  • Regular season: 7-9-1
  • Postseason: 1-2

While the numbers indicate teams have had slightly more success taking the ball first, the gap between the two strategies is small, just like the sample size.

That's part of why overtime strategies vary greatly from team-to-team. NFL coaches and decision-makers are still figuring out the new-look overtime, so it may be a couple of years before teams settle into a more universal, preferred strategy.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: To kick, or not to kick? NFL's new OT rules leave coaches with tough choice

item.title: The 3 biggest stars from the 49ers’ home opener: No rust for George Kittle
item.description: George Kittle, Nick Bosa, and Brock Purdy were the 3 stars for the 49ers in Week 2
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers took care of business, and that’s all you need to know about their home opener on Sunday.

The 49ers demolished the Miami Dolphins 35-13 in a game the Dolphins never had a chance in. Miami opened the game with a field goal, but the 49ers went on to outscore them 35-10 over the remaining 55 minutes.

San Francisco avoided a letdown spot after an impressive Week 1 win over the Rams and now carry the momentum of a 2-0 record into Week 3 against the Arizona Cardinals.

These are the three players most responsible for the 49ers’ second win of the season:

3rd Star: TE George Kittle

Allow me to be the first to mention that George Kittle tore his Achilles just nine months ago. He emphatically announced he’s healthy against Miami. 

Kittle led all pass-catchers with his 80 yards on four receptions, scoring one of two passing touchdowns for the 49ers on Sunday. But it was one drive in specific that helped Kittle en route to his monster day.

With the 49ers up eight to start the second half, San Francisco was looking to extend that lead early in the second half. That’s when Kyle Shanahan smashed the George Kittle button. The offense opened the third quarter with a quick strike to a wide-open Kittle for 40 yards, teleporting the 49ers into plus territory. Three plays later, Kittle scored his touchdown on a 12-yard pass to put the 49ers up 15 yards.

Kittle’s quick turnaround from such a devastating injury will continue to become more impressive with each week. If Week 1 was the first test of how Kittle could handle a real-speed game again, Sunday showed he can return to the level we’ve grown to expect from the tight end.

2nd Star: DE Nick Bosa

He didn’t collect a sack on Sunday, but Bosa wreaked havoc in the Miami backfield, forcing others to get to Malik Willis.

Osa Odighizuwa matched Bosa with four pressures against the Dolphins’ offensive line, but Bosa’s pressure caused issues for Willis. His first pressure of the game forced Willis to pass earlier than he wanted, resulting in an Upton Stout pass breakup. Later on the drive, Miami faced a third-and-goal, but when Bosa quickly got after Willis, the play quickly fell apart, and Bosa’s pressure led to Romello Height’s first-career sack.

His next pressure would result in Marques Sigle’s first career sack. With the 49ers up 21-6, the defense looked to put Miami away. Bosa beat Miami right tackle Austin Jackson off the snap and wrapped around the tackle, getting behind Willis. Willis stepped up in the pocket, but in the gap Bosa left, Sigle came through to finish the play and force the third down.

Bosa was effective in the run game in Week 1, but on Sunday, Bosa showed that pass-rush ability we’re familiar with.

1st Star: QB Brock Purdy

Miami’s secondary was leaving 49ers pass-catchers open all game, and Purdy happily took advantage. 

Purdy threw an incomplete pass to Deebo Samuel with 9:20 left in the first quarter. He then completed his next 18 passes. In those 18 passes, Purdy threw for 275 yards and two touchdowns, attacking the Dolphins’ defensive weaknesses. 

You could tell we were in for a good Purdy day on his fifth pass attempt of the game. With the 49ers offense facing a third-and-5, Miami pressure forced Purdy into a scramble drill. As usual, Purdy excelled on the off-script play. He kept the play alive with his feet before settling and hitting Mike Evans along the sidelines (with Evans making an acrobatic catch) for the first down. 

Purdy would have to wait for the second half for his touchdown pass when he connected with Kittle, and he’d close his scoring with a six-yard pass to Kyle Juszczyk to put the 49ers up 22 in the third quarter.

Oh, and did I mention Purdy led the 49ers in rushing yards? He gained all 30 yards on the same drive, with a 10-yard gain on his first carry followed by an 18-yard gain. His feet would close the drive, finishing his day on the ground with a two-yard score to put the 49ers up 14-3 in the second quarter.

 Purdy took what Miami was giving, and it resulted in a big day for the 49ers quarterback.

Throughout the season, we will track the three stars of the season by tallying points for each star award using a complex scoring system: three points for being the first star, two for the second, and one for the third. Through Week 2, the standings are:

  1. QB Brock Purdy – 5 points
  2. LB Fred Warner – 3 points
  3. DE Nick Bosa – 2 points

item.title: Aaron Glenn: No regrets about how we handled end of regulation against Packers
item.description: Jets head coach Aaron Glenn's late-game decision-making came under fire in Sunday's overtime loss to the Packers, but he doesn't feel any differently about his choices after a night to sleep on it.
item.content:encoded:
Jets head coach Aaron Glenn's late-game decision-making came under fire in Sunday's overtime loss to the Packers, but he doesn't feel any differently about his choices after a night to sleep on it.

After the 20-17 loss, Glenn said he never considered calling a timeout when the Packers faced a fourth down near midfield with about a minute left in regulation. The Packers wound up running the clock down and taking a delay of game penalty before trying a Hail Mary on the final snap of the game.

On Sunday, Glenn said he didn't want the team's offense to be backed up after a punt and reiterated that on a Monday video conference while expressing no doubt about the course of action he chose for the team.

"Between me and our game management guys, our analytical guys, we talk through those situations quite a bit," Glenn said. "That situation actually came up in a number of our conversations. When we have the punter at the logo, we don't want to put ourselves in a situation where we get our guys in a backed up situation. I know we talk about getting our offense going in that situation, but the thing is they had two timeouts also. If you put yourself in a backed up situation and things don't go as planned, I think you’re giving the other team an opportunity to go out there and make a play. I just felt like that was the right decision to do at that point and we actually wanted to play for overtime when it came to that.”

Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said on Sunday that he was "really confused" by how Glenn handled the situation, which could be translated to being really thankful that Glenn allowed the Packers to control how the final minute of regulation played out.

item.title: Chiefs’ Kahlil Benson is ‘winning over a lot of people,’ says Andy Reid
item.description: Kansas City’s rookie left tackle has impressed in filling in for the injured starter.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs are 2-0 through two weeks of the NFL season, and that has come with rookie Kahlil Benson at left tackle in place of the injured Josh Simmons (Back).

Last year’s starting right tackle at the University of Indiana has played every possible snap on the blind side so far, all 149 per Pro Football Focus, and has filled in admirably. He has allowed four hurries and two quarterback hits through two games, but hasn’t been faulted for any of the four sacks quarterback Patrick Mahomes has taken against the Denver Broncos and Indianapolis Colts.

He has held up on pass downs, with plenty of challenges to come if he stays in the lineup, but Benson’s run blocking has made him “one of the Chiefs’ five best linemen” right now, in the words of head coach Andy Reid before the season opener.

During the preseason, Chiefs offensive line coach Andy Heck said the coaching staff “could see [Benson] had dominant physical traits.” He has shown that off on run plays early on.

Benson shows off effortless power with his hands after climbing to the second level to nonchalantly pancake a Colts safety. The power he brings to blocks has stood out throughout practice and game observations.

He fires off the ball and uses that huge frame — 6 feet 6 inches tall with 34 1/2-inch arms — to create space for the Chiefs’ running backs. Running back Kenneth Walker had 10 carries to the left side of the line against Indianapolis; he totaled 69 rushing yards (6.9 yards per attempt) on those runs.

After the game, head coach Andy Reid acknowledged the rookie’s efforts.

“Yeah, there are a couple hiccups in there, but he was going against a good player,” Reid said to reporters. “And I thought he did a decent job… (General Manager Brett) Veach, great eyes, great eyes. I mean, to bring him in here, and then (Offensive Line Coach) Andy Heck believing in him and coaching him up, the kid believing in himself.

“I think he’s winning over a lot of people,” Reid said.

Is he winning over the coaching staff enough to keep him in the starting lineup? With Simmons’ return on the horizon, should we expect Benson to slide over to the right side?

Or does Benson stay in Simmons’ place regardless of the injury report? Right tackle Jaylon Moore didn’t allow a pressure over 51 pass blocks against the Colts, per PFF. He had a rougher performance in Week 1, but either way, the Chiefs will soon have to make decisions about their starting five up front.

item.title: Colts receive initial encouraging injury update on Alec Pierce, but further evaluation coming on Monday
item.description: The Colts could be without one of their top playmakers and downfield threats at least for a bit.
item.content:encoded:
According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler (which was later confirmed by head coach Shane Steichen post-game), the x-rays on Indianapolis Colts wideout Alec Pierce’s reinjured ankle/heel were negative last night:

However, further medical evaluation will be undergone on Monday, and given that Pierce was seen leaving Arrowhead Stadium in a boot and using crutches, I’m no doctor, but him missing time here again seems like a realistic possibility. It’s the same injured ankle/heel that kept him out of all of training camp and preseason.

Pierce left late in the first quarter on a non-contact play and was unable to put weight on his aggravated left ankle/heel, as he limped off to the sideline. He was eventually helped to the medical tent with the help of Colts team trainers before exiting the field entirely along the sidelines on a medical cart.

While he was initially designated as “questionable,” which seemed overly optimistic for any sort of return, he was quickly downgraded to “out” by the Colts medical staff—and obviously, was not available again last night.

Of course, it’s a big blow to the Colts offensively, as Pierce is one of their unit’s most explosive playmakers, and their best downfield threat—especially with their AFC South rival Houston Texans coming to town in Week 3.

The Colts absolutely want to avoid an 0-3 start and make an already increasingly large loss deficit, grow even bigger.

Even though the Texans defense has struggled a bit out of the gates, allowing the 24th most points (28.0 avg. ppg.) through two games in the 2026 campaign, reputationally, they’re still regarded as one of the league’s best.

With Pierce potentially absent, it could mean more looks for rookie Deion Burks downfield situationally, as well as Ashton Dulin (ankle), who’s also mending from an injury which kept him out of action last night.

Without Pierce’s deep speed and vertical separation, the Colts become a lot easier to cover, as none of the group of Keenan Allen, Josh Downs, or Tyler Warren are burners, which also means heavier boxes for Jonathan Taylor.

item.title: The Takeaway: Jalen Hurts can handle the heat
item.description: Philly’s star QB was a game-changing force in Tennessee.
item.content:encoded:
They wanted to make Jalen Hurts beat them as a quarterback.

That’s what Tennessee star defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons (who was a monster on Sunday) said about the Eagles’ star QB ahead of the Birds’ come-from-behind 24-20 win on Sunday that was orchestrated by Hurts’ arm and, in no small measure, a wonderful game by a wide receiver corps filled with question marks.

The plan was simple: keep Hurts in the pocket and, as Simmons said, “make Jalen Hurts be a QB.”

Hurts was not perfect. He almost never is. He threw two interceptions, one of which was almost returned for a 90+ yard pick-six and the other late in the fourth quarter as he was hit while he was throwing. They were uncharacteristic of him, but in the new Sean Mannion offense, we may have to get used to things like this.

But for most of the game and, most importantly, in their final drive, Hurts was masterful. He was 26-for-37 passing with 264 yards and two touchdowns and, with under two minutes remaining and trailing 20-17, went 6-for-8 on a 65-yard drive that culminated in 3-yard touchdown to Darius Cooper with 9 seconds left.

It was not an easy game. The Titans were fired up and the Eagles had never won a game in Tennessee since the Houston Oilers moved to Nissan Stadium in 1999. It was also about 357 degrees Farenheit on the field. Players’ cleats were melting.

Hurts also had to deal with an offensive line that is still finding its footing in the new Mannion scheme. He was under pressure for much of the day, yet managed to pass his way through it.

With Landon Dickerson out, the Eagles moved Cam Jurgens from center to left guard and started Drew Kendall at center. That didn’t seem to work out too well. The running game provided little support, averaging 2.8 yards per attempt. Saquon Barkley missed almost the entire first half with a stinger and finished with just 9 yards on 4 attempts. Tank Bigsby scored a touchdown on the ground but managed just 33 yards on 13 carries. Will Shipley added 24 yards on 7 carries.

So, it was all on Hurts.

Hurts threw over the middle of the field more, threading the needle in some cases and layering passes over linebackers in others. There were times he took too long to get rid of the ball, but also seemed more inclined to let it rip than in seasons past.

He was also aided by his top two veteran wide receivers, as well as a second-year training camp star.

DeVonta Smith showed why everyone was excited for him to take over as WR1. He hauled in 10 of his 13 targets for 117 yards and a touchdown, making several acrobatic catches in traffic along the way. Especially clutch was his last catch of the day on the final drive.

One of the more important developments early in the season is the play of Dontayvion Wicks, who is emerging as a more-than viable No. 2. He caught 5 of his 6 targets for 74 yards, including a 27-yarder that helped get the Eagles’ offense moving early.

And while Cooper did not pile up big stats on Sunday, he did come up with the biggest catch of the day in the game’s final seconds, and even Makai Lemon showed up with a clutch 14-yard catch. Hurts completed passes to nine different players, an offensive coordinator’s dream.

Hurts will never be confused with Joe Montana, but he is proving to be one of the most adaptable QBs in franchise history. It’s only been two games, and we haven’t truly seen Mannion’s offense “work” yet. The running game needs to be functional in order for that to happen. In the meantime, Hurts is doing more than enough inside the system and, improvisationally, to win.

Yes, it feels a lot like last year still. It seems unlikely the Eagles are going be blowing people out this year, at least not yet. In the meantime, Hurts is showing that, after an off-season of uncertainty, he can handle the heat.

item.title: Will Rams enter the NFC West race on Monday Night Football?
item.description: It’s been two games for most, and the Los Angeles Rams are behind, and more NFL news on a Monday
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams are already behind the Seattle Seahawks, San Francisco 49ers and the Arizona Cardinals in the NFC West race with L.A.’s Week 2 game still to be played on Monday night. Even with a win Monday, the Rams will still be looking up at the 49ers and Seahawks, but a win puts the Rams back in business with a 1-1 record.

An 0-2 record could mean the end of their season. Yes, that’s dramatic, and, yes, it could be true. I don’t make the rules. The rules are you need to win the in the NFL and so far, the Rams haven’t. Can they put a winning game together on Monday night?

Even if the Rams lose, what fans and the team want to see is a better effort than they showed in Week 1. If L.A. comes out flat, or just plain bad again, the concern meter will rise.

Will Matthew Stafford look better? Can the Rams overcome the loss of Myles Garrett? How does Aaron Donald look? Will Puka Nacua play? If Nacua doesn’t play, how will the Rams respond? Can Chris Shula and his defense improve? How about Harrison Mevis and the special teams?

The Rams have a lot of questions. They get the chance to answer some of them (for better or worse) on Monday Night Football.

2026 NFL season, Week 2: What We Learned from Sunday’s games (nfl.com)

“Mike Macdonald’s defense smothers Cardinals. Arizona had one good drive – a 12-play, 61-yard, five-first down, TD possession – in the first half. The rest of the afternoon, Seattle’s defense dominated. The defensive line destroyed the Cards’ front, bringing waves of pressure and slamming the door on Arizona’s running game. Seattle allowed just 39 yards on 14 carries combined from Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier (2.8 yards per carry). With the run game silenced, Seattle was able to tee off on Jacoby Brissett. The Seahawks generated 18 QB pressures, per Next Gen Stats. On dropbacks under pressure, Seattle held Brissett to 4 of 11 for 9 yards, with an interception and a 7.0 passer rating. Give safety Julian Love some flowers for a gorgeous sliding INT, his second of the season. Facing a Cards team that put up nearly 400 yards in Week 1, Macdonald’s crew held Arizona to 151 yards, 3.2 yards per play, 10 first downs and 3 of 12 on third downs. Domination.“

2026 NFL season, Week 2: What We Learned from Sunday’s games (nfl.com)

“Milestone day for McCaffrey, Kittle. On a day that was all about Kyle Shanahan’s offense, it was no shock that the heartbeat of the supporting cast shined brightest. Christian McCaffrey had just 67 scrimmage yards but made the most of his touches near the goal line. His pair of rushing scores put him in elite company, as he became the third player in NFL history to record 50-plus scrimmage TDs with multiple teams, joining Hall of Famers Marshall Faulk (Rams, 85; Colts 51) and Randy Moss (Vikings, 92; Patriots, 50). But perhaps the most exciting aspect of San Francisco’s offensive frenzy was George Kittle’s return to prominence. After missing six games in 2025 with an Achilles injury and a modest Week 1 outing in Australia, the seven-time Pro Bowler led the team with 80 receiving yards and his first touchdown, a 12-yard reception on a busted coverage, since the injury. Kittle’s third catch of the day also marked his 600th career reception, the 11th tight end in league history to accomplish that feat.“

Whose house? Rams return home as Aaron Donald makes long-awaited comeback against Giants (nypost)

“The Rams surrendered 174 rushing yards, failed to record a sack on 34 pass attempts and generated just two quarterback hits. Myles Garrett finished with the same statistical line as Aaron Donald, who watched from the comforts of his couch at home in Los Angeles: zero tackles, zero sacks and zero pressures.

Now Garrett is on injured reserve following a knee procedure, leaving Donald to make his anticipated return after more than two years away from football.

The rams have 99 problems, but No. 99 will not be one, no pressure AD.“

Notable injuries, news from Sunday’s Week 2 games: Packers WR Jayden Reed (neck) carted off vs. Jets (nfl.com)

“San Francisco 49ers receiver Demarcus Robinson (ankle) was ruled out of Sunday’s game against the Dolphins. Head coach Kyle Shanahan told reporters after the game Robinson and DT James Thompson Jr. have high ankle sprains. Wide receiver Mike Evans (hip) did not return to the game but the injury doesn’t look serious, per Shanahan.

Seattle Seahawks running back Jadarian Price (chest) did not return to Sunday’s game against the Cardinals. HC Mike Macdonald said after the game that X-rays came back negative on Price’s injury.“

New York Giants vs. Rams: 5 things to know before Monday night’s kickoff (giantswire)

“Donald will be strapping on the pads for the first time since 2023, having retired after that season. No one knows what kind of physical or mental shape he’s in, what impact he’ll have, or how much he’ll play. He’ll be butting heads with Giants rookie guard Francis Mauigoa, which promises to be an interesting matchup.

Nacua has been nursing a groin injury and is listed as questionable. He did not practice Saturday, but his track record suggests he’ll play. At what percentage is unknown. If Puka is limited, the Rams don’t have much depth behind him, with Jordan Whittington (quad) doubtful. Of course, they still have Davante Adams in their lineup, but he only caught three of six targets in the Week 1 loss to San Francisco.“

Donald in, Garrett out: How will Rams defense look with huge addition (and subtraction)? (espn)

“Though the future Pro Football Hall of Fame defensive tackle said he knows it has been two full seasons since he walked off the field after the season-ending loss to the Detroit Lions, in a way, it feels like he never left.

“[After] being back around, I feel like I was just here last year,” Donald said. “Time flies by so fast, and I forget that I haven’t play[ed] football for two years. I feel like I’m just back to my normal self.”

Donald did not play in — or even travel to — the Rams’ season-opening loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, Australia, as he worked to get up to speed after coming out of retirement Aug. 30.“

Giants vs. Rams: What to watch as Los Angeles looks to bounce back in ‘MNF’ (cbsports)

“The Giants did whatever they wanted against the Cowboys on “Sunday Night Football” last weekend. New York ran the ball 37 times for 165 yards and a touchdown. Jaxson Dart completed 23 of 29 passes for 230 yards and three scores. The Giants controlled the ball for 36 minutes and 40 seconds of the 60-minute game. They had three second-half drives; they scored a touchdown on each of the first two and ran the clock out on the third. All three drives lasted 12-plus plays. It was surgical stuff.“

Sean McVay and Rams are being tested early, but it’s far too soon to write them off (nytimes)

“The numbers speak to the depths of that performance, but also to the standard that made the Rams Super Bowl favorites even before their blockbuster trade for two-time Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett or the return of three-time Defensive Player of the Year Aaron Donald from retirement.

Unlike some infamous preseason “dream teams,” these Rams weren’t microwaved through transactions in a single offseason. This team fell just short of a trip to the Super Bowl and returned every starter except the two it replaced with Garrett and All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie.“

Criticism of Chris Shula Is Missing the Bigger Picture With Rams Defense (si.com)

“However, that doesn’t make the defense blameless. The Rams trailed by three points at halftime before the 49ers scored a touchdown to start the half and then allowed a 99-yard touchdown drive following a missed fourth-down conversion from the offense.

Put together, it simply wasn’t good complementary football. The defense was certainly put in a bad position with a long kick return to start the second half. Despite the offense not scoring from the one-yard line, the defense needs to find a way to get a stop. It wasn’t just one unit that deserved blame, but all three phases.

That doesn’t mean that multiple things can’t be true. Yes, more is expected from the offensive side of the ball. At the same time, there are places where the defense can be better.“

“New York’s opener was sharp. Jaxson Dart completed 23 of 29 passes for 230 yards and three touchdowns without an interception, added 11 carries for 54 yards, and Isaiah Likely caught all eight of his targets for 78 yards and two scores.

Los Angeles never got going in Australia. Matthew Stafford finished 15 of 25 for 155 yards with no touchdowns and one interception, while Puka Nacua still led the Rams with five catches for 74 yards.

The Rams are 7-point favorites over the Giants, with a total of 48.5 and a moneyline of -356 for the Rams and +283 for the Giants. Keep reading for everything you need to tune in.“

Comment of the Day:

I expect the Giants to move the ball well and my only real concern is our secondary.

I think most Giants fans are looking at this game as a free swing at a SB contender.“-Haggis64
