item.title: Ravens vs. Saints: 4 winners and plenty of losers
item.description: The Ravens have plenty of blame to share in their loss to the Saints
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens fell back to earth this week with a humbling loss to the New Orleans Saints. There was plenty of blame to go around in this one, with a few bright spots mixed in.

Winners

Rashod Bateman: The Ravens needed their former first-rounder to step up in Zay Flowers’ absence this week, and Bateman answered the call with 88 receiving yards and a touchdown on seven catches. Bateman was the intended target on Lamar Jackson’s game-sealing interception, leading to questions about whether he ran the correct route, but both players were quick to shut such speculation down after the game.

Trenton Simpson: Simpson’s contract season is off to a strong start through two games. The athletic linebacker was everywhere against the Saints, making six tackles and one tackle for loss. Simpson helped end several plays close to the line of scrimmage throughout the game.

Mark Andrews: Andrews started the game on the wrong foot with a drop on third down, leading to a three-and-out on the offense’s first series. The veteran tight end rebounded afterwards, though, moving the chains on multiple plays and helping to spring several runs with key blocks. Andrews finished the day with 49 yards on six catches. While he may not be the explosive threat he once was, Jackson’s career go-to target can still be a reliable option through the air.

Devontez Walker: Walker had just one catch on the day, but it was a big one. Backed up in their own end zone, Jackson connected with Walker on a 47-yard bomb. Walker has done nothing but make big plays when called upon so far in his career.

Losers

Secondary: Just about every member of the secondary shares some blame, from allowing Chris Olave to convert multiple key first downs to missing crucial tackles throughout the game. Safeties Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins seemed to be the worst offenders, with both missing tackles that led to extended drives for New Orleans. Starks appeared to be responsible for Olave’s touchdown catch as well.

Special teams: The Ravens’ special teams had multiple gaffes on the day, the first being a blocked field goal that would have given Baltimore a 10-0 lead in the second quarter. Perhaps the bigger blunder, though, was allowing a 53-yard kick return before the end of the first half that allowed the Saints to cut the lead to eight with a field goal.

Coaching staff: The honeymoon period for the Ravens’ new coaching staff is officially over. Sunday’s loss featured multiple questionable decisions on both sides of the ball. Possibly the biggest head-scratcher of the day was opting for a deep shot to wide receiver Chris Moore on third-and-one instead of handing the ball to Derrick Henry. The incomplete pass led to a three-and-out while the game was tied in the fourth quarter. Jesse Minter also had a questionable challenge on an Olave catch on the previous drive, which led to the Ravens only having two timeouts with just over a minute left on their final drive of the game.

Chris Moore: Moore was the surprising hero of Week 1, but things did not go as well this week for the veteran receiver. Moore was the intended target on the aforementioned third-and-one deep ball, failing to haul the pass in. Moore was also flagged for holding earlier in the game, which negated a signature Jackson scramble for a first down. Moore nearly fumbled on a kickoff return as well, but he was ruled down on replay.

item.title: 5 Bears Takes: Waiting on a Williams update, red zone failures, and good defense?
item.description: Sunday’s game went from frustrating to panic in the matter of one play. Here are five takes after the Bears’ first loss from @AaronLemingNFL.
item.content:encoded:
Week 2 of the NFL delivered another outstanding weekend of football, but the offense was much harder to find for most teams. Unfortunately, the Chicago Bears were one of those teams, putting up just three points over 60 minutes of football. Despite a final score of 9-3 not going their way, all eyes are on the health of quarterback Caleb Williams, who left in the fourth quarter what appeared to be a serious hamstring injury. At (1-1) and (0-1) within the division, how they fare over the next few weeks (or maybe more) will determine how competitive they can be in November and December. For more on a disastrous Sunday and how to move forward, let’s dive into our weekly postgame Bears Takes. 

1. Although head coach Ben Johnson was noncommittal during his postgame presser, Monday’s MRI results for Caleb Williams might dictate how serious of a contender the Bears can be moving forward this season. The early reports are promising, though.

Even with a strong performance from the defense on Sunday, it was fair to say that the Bears’ ceiling was going to be dictated by how well they were able to settle in after a rough Week 1 against the Carolina Panthers. With Williams out for the foreseeable future, the road back to the playoffs became that much harder. According to NBC Sports’ Mike Florio, there’s optimism that Williams suffered a Grade 1 sprain, which would keep him out only a few weeks.

Outside of Florio, both Johnson and the top insiders have echoed the same information: Williams will have an MRI on Monday to determine the severity of his hamstring injury. Given how bad it looked in real time, anything short of season-ending would feel like a big “win” for the long term. That said, anything that avoids injured reserve should keep the Bears in the playoff race.

For what it’s worth, the Seahawks are in a very similar position with Sam Darnold leaving Week 1 with a glute injury. They are also trying to keep their heads above water, but the initial thought is that Darnold will return before Williams. Sunday’s loss (which we’ll touch on more later) was tough enough, but it’s worth keeping in mind that navigating this at 2-0 with a divisional win is a lot easier than what they are currently facing. 

To muddy the waters even more, this will be the first time that Johnson will be calling plays relying on a backup quarterback. The offense will need to change moving forward, but relying on their run game will be key to finding offensive success. For now, we’ll wait for a more concrete timeline and hope it’s on the shorter end of everyone’s feared timeline. 

2. Even before Williams’ injury, the offense was getting their brains beat out by Vikings’ defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Like we pounded home last week, overreacting to Week 1 rarely works out well. Plenty of other teams struggled around the league to follow up their season-opening performances. 

All week, we heard about the battle between Johnson and Flores. For outside observers, I’m sure it’s a great chess match to watch twice a year, but for Bears fans, it hasn’t been overly fun since Johnson came over from Detroit. Despite their 59-point performance last week, the offense struggled all day to move the ball. Even when they were in position to score, it backfired every time except for their first-quarter field goal. 

Williams had one of his worst games in quite some time, but he was far from the only disappointment on Sunday. The run game struggled to get going consistently. For all the explosive plays they had last week, many more runs went for less than two yards in their home opener. 

More concerning, their receivers weren’t getting open, and the offensive line wasn’t holding up in pass protection against the blitz. To be fair, Flores blitzed over 70% of the time, but even so, this offense has proven it can succeed against that approach in the past. The offensive line is down two starters from last season, but even so, they looked disjointed for most of the game. 

Despite all their issues, they still had multiple chances to put points on the board and simply couldn’t. The goal-line fumble from D’Andre Swift felt like a back-breaker in the moment, but the blocked field goal felt like a week-long issue in the making. Rookie long snapper Beau Gardner has shown a tendency to snap the ball high, but the blocking off the edges was shaky last weekend against the Panthers, too. 

While these are the types of games that feel like they are simply impossible, Johnson and this offense will now be tasked with getting back on track against another tough defense on a national stage next Monday night. Figuring out the penalties will be key, but their execution in “scoring position” must also vastly improve. Now they’ll be doing that with a backup quarterback under center. 

3. The defense was far from perfect, but if you had told anyone earlier in the week that they gave up just nine points and no touchdowns, everyone would have assumed the Bears won in a blowout. 

There aren’t going to be many “pretty” performances from this defensive group, but this was about as good a day as anyone should realistically ask for in 2026. Allowing an aging Aaron Jones to go for 105 yards on 23 carries isn’t ideal, but allowing just 127 total passing yards, three sacks, and no touchdowns should be enough for almost any team to win a game. 

That said, maybe we shouldn’t be as surprised. After all, Carson Wentz has been responsible for handing some ugly losses to the Bears. Before Sunday, the last time he started a game and beat the Bears was when the Bears couldn’t overcome a 12-point defensive effort, in which they had multiple cracks inside the five on Thursday night football. 

Regardless of the Brock Osweiler-type black magic, the defense played more than well enough to come out with a victory on Sunday. Still, it didn’t happen thanks to some very uncharacteristic struggles from the offense. On the plus side, their performance should give fans hope that they won’t set bad records and that being closer to league-average isn’t out of the question. If we are being honest, their best shot at staying afloat might be playing as close to league-average as possible, with Williams expected to be on the shelf for a while. 

4. For years, we’ve heard how good of a backup Tyson Bagent is. With Williams out for the foreseeable future, we’ll see if he can keep the Bears in the mix. It’s also worth noting that this will be Johnson’s first time navigating these waters, too. 

Simply put, the Bears’ immediate playoff hopes (even heading into Week 3) will ride on how much Johnson can get out of his backup quarterback. The team has loved him since he came in as an undrafted free agent from Shepherd. He’s survived through two head coaches and is just a little over a year removed from signing a two-year extension. 

Regardless of what anyone wants to believe, the difference between Williams and Bagent is very different. While Bagent has some mobility in his game, the stark difference in arm strength will be extremely noticeable. That doesn’t mean Bagent can’t succeed. In fact, Johnson’s vote of confidence in him should give Bears fans plenty of hope that with some modifications to the offense, they can still do more than enough to win games. 

I expect the offense will become more of a “quick strike” unit that relies on quick, decisive reads and, of course, a strong run game. That might help the offensive line get into a better rhythm, but the big-play aspects of this unit might be less consistent. Think more of what Johnson did in Detroit with Goff as a better example. 

How long Williams is out will also matter. Initial speculation (from Twitter doctors) puts Williams’ return-to-play timeframe in the three-to-six-week window. Assuming the middle point of the target, it would leave three-to-four games for Bagent to cover. Here’s how that schedule looks:

Vs Eagles (2-0)

Vs Jets (1-1)

At Packers (1-1)

At Falcons (0-2)

If that goes further into the six-to-eight week timeframe, here’s how the next four games would look:

Vs Patriots (1-1)

At Seahawks (2-0)

Vs Buccaneers (0-2)

Vs Saints (1-1)

Going .500 might cut it over four games (if Williams is out that long); anything more will likely require a winning record. Can Bagent and the Bears keep their heads above water while they wait for the franchise quarterback to return? Without mincing words, it’ll dictate how successful their 2026 season will be. 

5a. NFC North Lookaround: The Detroit Lions were run out of Highmark Stadium on Thursday Night Football, the Green Bay Packers broke their six-game losing streak, and the Vikings stand alone in first place following Sunday’s win at Soldier Field. 

The NFC North helped kick off the first Thursday Night Football game of the season, and unfortunately for the Lions, it did not go well… At all. Disregard the 41-31 score (if you didn’t get a chance to watch) because the game was never close. The Buffalo Bills jumped out to a 21-0 lead before the Lions were able to catch their breath. Despite a 10-point margin when looking at the final score, Detroit’s inability to stop the Bills’ offense (two punts in nine drives) put their offense in a position where they were consistently fighting from behind all night. Through two games, it’s clear the Lions’ defense is an issue, as they’ve given up 71 points and over 900 total yards through two games. The talent is there, and the schedule should be advantageous, but they’ve got plenty to work through over the next month-plus if they plan on competing for a playoff spot in December and beyond. 

After blowing another fourth-quarter lead in Minnesota that led to quite the turbulent week in Green Bay, the Packers were back at it on Sunday afternoon against the upstart Jets, who were looking for their first 2-0 start since 2015. Yes, you read that right- 2015. Todd Bowles was the head coach and Ryan Fitzpatrick was the starting quarterback. Despite leading for the majority of the game, the Jets’ offense stalled in the fourth quarter and could not get things going again in overtime. For the Packers, their six-game losing streak going back to last year is over. With a favorable matchup on a short week against the Atlanta Falcons, the Packers appear to be back on track in a wide-open division. 

It wasn’t pretty, and despite two straight divisional victories to open up the season, the Vikings will be thrilled to welcome back quarterback Kyler Murray, assuming he clears concussion protocol ahead of Week 3. It wasn’t pretty on Sunday, but in typical Minnesota fashion, they found ways to keep the Bears out of the end zone and do just enough offensively to come away with the big road victory. Despite many picking them to finish last in the division, me included, they are pacing the NFC North and have a great head start. 

Here are the standings after Week 2:

(2-0) Minnesota Vikings 

(1-1) Detroit Lions 

(1-1) Chicago Bears

(1-1) Green Bay Packers

5b. Week 3 Look Ahead: A Monday Night Football rematch with the Philadelphia Eagles, where they’ll look to atone for their Black Friday loss last year, and it’ll likely be against Bagent.

Despite some personnel shakeup this offseason, the Eagles are off to a 2-0 start, even if they didn’t look great in either game. That said, their defense is still very good, and Bears fans should assume that defensive coordinator Vic Fangio is going to have plenty of confusing looks for Bagent starting his first game in four seasons. 

So far, the Eagles appear to be benefiting from two poor opponents. While the defense has done its job, something still feels missing from the offense. Quarterback Jalen Hurts has been OK, but he turned the ball over twice against the Titans, and if not for a last-minute touchdown, they’d be heading into Chicago at (1-1). 

Because of the quarterback discrepancy, the Eagles will be favored (as of Sunday night, it’s 4.5 points), but the Bears can win if they clean up many of their mistakes from Sunday. While this won’t be as big of a game for the Eagles considering their 2-0 start, a win on Monday night for the Bears would not only help out their conference record but also get them one game closer to getting their starting quarterback back in the mix.

item.title: Week 2 AFC West roundup, Kansas City Chiefs’ overtime win keeps pace with Las Vegas
item.description: Raiders were a second away from having sole possession of the division lead.
item.content:encoded:
The Las Vegas Raiders have plenty of momentum in the AFC West after a big Week 2 win over a division rival, the Los Angeles Chargers, which keeps the Raiders in first place and pushes the Chargers to the bottom of the standings at 0-2. On that note, let’s check in on how the Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs fared on Sunday.

Broncos vs. Jaguars

Score: 20-13 Broncos win

Key Stats:

  • QB Bo Nix: 22/31 (71.0%), 288 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT
  • RB Jonah Coleman: 10 carries, 39 yards, 1 TD
  • WR Jaylen Waddle: 8 catches, 138 yards
  • DT Malcolm Roach: 4 tackles, 1 sack, 2 QB hits, 2 TFLs
  • CB Riley Moss: 2 tackles, 3 PDs

Unlike the Chargers, the Denver Broncos managed to escape and avoid digging themselves into a 0-2 hole during their home opener on Sunday. But “escape” is the keyword there, as Denver trailed by two possessions early in the second half and didn’t take the lead until about halfway through the fourth quarter. The Broncos haven’t looked very impressive during the first two weeks, getting blown out by the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 1. Then again, they have played a pair of good opponents, and this is a team that one-possession won its way to a 14-3 record and the AFC Championship last year. The scary part about Denver’s victory over Jacksonville is that Waddle, the club’s big offseason addition, announced his presence on Sunday.

Kansas City’s defense showed some cracks, giving up 119 rushing yards (92 to Jonathan Taylor) and 30 points while failing to sack Indianapolis Colts’ quarterback Daniel Jones. However, the Chiefs’ offense appears to be back after a couple of down years, especially with Walker accounting for nearly 180 yards from scrimmage after 191 last week. That could set up for an interesting battle at Allegiant Stadium in a couple of weeks…

  • Raiders look well-coached: “But, they were, by far, the better, more efficient team Sunday as they beat the Los Angeles Chargers 26-14 to improve to 2-0 under new head coach Klint Kubiak,” S&BP’s Bill Williamson wrote. “…Yes, it’s early, but the Raiders appear to be a much improved team and, just as importantly, a well-coached team by Kubiak and his staff.”

item.title: Heading into Chargers game, Bills can’t forget about this phenomenon
item.description: This can’t be dismissed before Bills-Chargers in Week 3
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers will enter this Week 3 contested headed in diametrically opposed directions, which can often spawn a rather silly assumption.

That we are sure of something in the NFL, especially in September.

Now, should the Bills have confidence going into this game? Yes. Plenty of it. And, I’ll never blame for a team for, internally, feeling good about their chances against a team spiraling as opposed to an opponent firing on all cylinders.

But we can’t simply assume this game is over before it begins.

There’s too much parity in today’s NFL.

And many times, right when we collectively feel like we have a team or teams figured out, the unexpected strikes.

Justin Herbert defenders are going through it to begin the 2026 season. He’s completed 59.3% of his throws, with two touchdowns and three interceptions and has been sacked six times in this 0-2 start. That comes after another dud of a playoff game last January.

Mike McDaniels’ widely regarded reputation as an offensive genius is continuing to lose luster, fast, and it’s fair to start to wonder if Jim Harbaugh, at this age, can be a Super Bowl-caliber coach.

But Herbert has insane big-time throw ability in him. McDaniels did coach a Dolphins team that, with plenty of talent, saw Tua Tagovailoa lead the NFL in passer rating. Derwin James has been a first or second team All-Pro six times. And Harbaugh has won everywhere he’s coached, from FCS football to Stanford to Michigan to the 49ers.

Heck, McDaniels’ rather hapless Dolphins trounced the Bills 30-13 in November last season.

And, for the Bills, the Patriots are coming to town in Week 4. This Sunday could be referred to as a “trap game.” Buffalo can’t get caught looking ahead. Because for as much as the Chargers may very well be already into a season-long implosion with some polarizing yet previously successful characters at the top of their organization, the bounce-back tendency of the NFL cannot be forgotten before this Week 3 game.

It’s very real. Sure, favorites can cruise. But more often than we initially believe, two teams playing each other one week do not resemble what we’ve previously seen from them.

However, I’ll end with this — if Buffalo can get out to a sizable lead in the first half, this does feel like a Chargers team that won’t have nearly as much fight in it as the Lions showed in Week 2.

item.title: Eagles' Nick Sirianni needs IV, players report melting cleats vs. Titans
item.description: Amid record-setting heat wave in Nashville, players have cleats sprayed with water, Eagles coach Nick Sirianni requires IV as turf temperatures soar.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans are moving into a new stadium next season. Hopefully, the turf there won't be as hot as the surface of Venus.

On-field temperatures hit 157 degrees during the third quarter of Sunday's game against the Philadelphia Eagles, according to the Fox Sports broadcast, with some players getting their cleats sprayed with water during timeouts.

Eagles coach Nick Sirianni even had to have IV fluids administered after the game.

"It was hot as (expletive)," Sirianni said, per ESPN. "I didn't play a snap and I had to get an IV. I so appreciate how much the guys prepared. I so appreciate how much they fought through because it wasn't easy."

Reason Number 100 why
Natural Grass > Field Turf

135+ Degrees on the field turf in Nashville pic.twitter.com/m4fDyh0NVq

— Chris Law (@ChrisLaw) September 20, 2026

Eagles offensive lineman Cam Jurgens said he went through multiple pairs of cleats during the game because the scorching hot Field Turf at Nissan Stadium was melting the soles.

The Eagles ended up defeating the Titans 24-20 on a last-second touchdown pass from Jalen Hurts to Darius Cooper.

"This is why we want all grass fields," said Eagles tackle Jordan Mailata, the team's NFL Players Association rep, "to create a standard of play in the league where we're not putting players in dangerous positions if we don't have to."

Mailata said he rolled his ankles twice during the game, an issue he said could have been because his cleats had partially melted.

In the wake of a record heat wave, the game-time temperature in Nashville for the noon kickoff was 95 degrees, with a heat index of 105.

item.content:encoded:
The Houston Texans’ 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals stung in a way that is a bit rattling to those that were hoping for a breakthrough season. It’s still a bit early, but maybe the Texans’ 0-2 start has shaken your faith in this team and their championship ambitions. They’ve played poorly enough to warrant this doubt, but one of the great things about the NFL is that they’re one good game away from turning the page on this rough start. Next week, the Texans will play their first road game when they travel up north to play the 0-2 Indianapolis Colts in an early divisional bout to determine who’s racing to the bottom of the AFC faster. It’s an early-season battle between the AFC South’s disturbing cousins, and FanDuel has got their opening odds for the game:

What may have been seen as an easier game for Houston before the season started has now become far more intimidating, especially after Indy’s overtime loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. FanDuel is narrowly favoring the Texans to win over the Colts in this game, meaning the Texans haven’t quite returned to the underdog status that they occupied for the majority of last season. They certainly aren’t the world-beaters many expected of them coming into 2026, and FanDuel has taken note of the disappointing results, but despite it all, they are still favored in this game.

THE SPREAD: TEXANS -2.5

Since the Texans are -2.5, FanDuel is expecting the Texans to win, but still expects the game to be close. That’s encouraging for Houston, and historically, this era of the Texans have been dominant against the Colts. They swept the Colts last year, and in his career, Texans QB CJ Stroud is 5-1 against Indianapolis, his only loss coming in 2023. This season, Stroud has been one of the few bright spots on the team thus far, and I expect him to continue his dominance over the Colts and their suspect pass-defense. Jonathan Taylor will likely feast on the Texans, but Houston’s offense should be able to maintain a lead on Indianapolis. Colts WR Pierce’s status for Week 3 following the team’s loss to the Chiefs Sunday night is in serious doubt, so I think the Texans will rebound and get this season back on track. I’m taking the spread here! Watch out!

THE MONEY LINE: Texans -146

Between these two admittedly sloppy and injured squads, the Texans are narrowly favored. If you were to bet $14.60 on the Texans winning, you’d net $10.00 in return. After that Bengals game, I don’t blame you if you’re against betting on the Texans to win any game, but last time the Texans played the Colts, they won in a shootout in the 2025 season finale 38-30 on just 339 total yards – 35 less than they gained against the Bengals yesterday. That Texans win came from the efforts of a lot of backup players that Houston plugged into the game following the first half – which may bode well considering the amount of backups that will be playing next week’s game due to Houston’s alarming number of injuries. KPRC2’s Aaron Wilson reported that it’s possible both WR Nico Collins and RG Ed Ingram miss two games following their respective hamstring and groin injuries, so Houston’s depth at those positions will be tested yet again.

Still, Houston’s recent history of success against Indianapolis gives me optimism despite the critical injuries. Their history against the Colts must be influencing FanDuel since Houston is still favored despite all of their warts. They should have at least a moderately improved rushing attack against the Colts, and that should grant the Texans a far more complimentary offense – so give me the Texans to win it!

OVER/UNDER: 44.5

Honestly, as much as I wish for the over to occur, I expect this game to actually stay below 44.5 total points. Both the Texans and Colts have had a lot of drives end in field goals in the first two games, and, following Colts WR Alec Pierce’s injury during Sunday Night Football, both teams will now be missing their #1 receiver in this Week 3 matchup. That means a lot more handoffs and loaded boxes. Both teams will get production from their quarterbacks, but I expect a lot of drives to stall in the red zone. Give me the Texans to win 23-20.

item.title: Eagles and Titans players had their cleats melting in 157-degree heat
item.description: Temperatures were dangerous in Nashville on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
A heatwave in Nashville paired with the Nissan Stadium turf created one of the most astonishing events to occur on a football field, Sunday — as the Philadelphia Eagles and Tennessee Titans quite literally had their cleats melting while playing in Week 2.

With air temperatures over 95 degrees at kickoff it created a scenario where the turn itself was measured at 157 degrees — enough to melt the mid-sole of cleats, which led the Eagles to spraying water on players’ feet in an effort to keep the integrity of their footwear.

Not only did players see their cleats physically melting on the field, but the heat caused the composition of the cleats to change, with Jordan Mailata saying that he rolled his ankle twice on Sunday — and believed it could have been caused by the plastic of his cleats becoming soft due to the heat.

Conditions were so extreme that Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni got an IV at halftime to prevent dehydration, which came from just standing on the surface for 90 minutes. Players struggled to keep cool, and it’s raising more questions about player safety due to weather-related events, especially as it pertains to playing surfaces.

Artificial turf of all kinds trap heat, but field turf is particularly egregious. Natural grass sheds heat through evaporative cooling, but both the turf itself and the rubber substrate absorb heat energy and have no way of getting rid of it. It’s for this reason the field temperature was 60 degrees higher than air temp on Sunday, which is considered normal for the playing surface.

Mailata, the Eagles player representative to the NFLPA, told ESPN that this is part of the reason the union is pushing for teams to move to grass surfaces league-wide.

“I’ve never thought about how hot a stadium can be if it’s turf. [The heat] just sits there and bounces up into you,” Mailata said. “We’ve got to bring it up. This is why we want all grass fields, to create a standard of play in the league where we’re not putting players in dangerous positions if we don’t have to.”

Something had to change long-term. The idea that NFL athletes are being pressured into playing with melted cleats is unacceptable. Either the field surface needs to change to make things cooler, or the league needs to force teams to add cooling technology under their playing surfaces so this doesn’t happen.

item.title: Dak Prescott: "Super honored" to set Cowboys TD record, want to double it
item.description: Dak Prescott owned most of the career quarterbacking records for the Cowboys before Sunday's game against the Commanders kicked off and he broke one of the other ones late in the fourth quarter.
item.content:encoded:
Dak Prescott owned most of the career quarterbacking records for the Cowboys before Sunday's game against the Commanders kicked off and he broke one of the other ones late in the fourth quarter.

Prescott's 24-yard touchdown pass to CeeDee Lamb was the 249th of his career, which broke a tie with Tony Romo for the most of any player in Cowboys history. It also put the finishing touches on a 37-20 Cowboys win and Prescott discussed how much the record means to him while wearing a Roger Staubach jersey at his postgame press conference.

Prescott also said he hopes to add a lot more touchdowns to the ledger before he's done in Dallas.

"I'm blessed, honored," Prescott said, via the team's website. "As I told you earlier in the week, records are meant to be broken. This is my time to break this one. Pretty cool to do it against the team I threw my first touchdown against ten years ago or so. Definitely humbling, something I don't take for granted. The great history of this organization, of the past quarterbacks before me. . . . Super, super honored. Super thankful. God's great. Not taking it lightly. But as I told you, it's just the beginning. I want to double it and plan to play for a while, so just getting started."

Prescott's place in the franchise record book will be secure regardless of what happens from here, but his place in the history of the franchise overall is still lacking the signature postseason wins that predecessors like Staubach and Troy Aikman have in their bios. Sunday's win doesn't rank at that level, but it helps the Cowboys' bid to get Prescott in position to deliver one.
